reader_summary.overview: I'm Patrick O'Shaughnessy, and this is Invest Like the Best. This show is an open-ended exploration of markets, ideas, methods, stories, and of strategies that will help you better invest both your time and your money. You can learn more and stay up to date at investorfieldguide.com.

thesis: This episode argues that investors should prioritize companies with high incremental returns on capital and management teams incentivized by long-term, capital-based metrics rather than nonsensical top-line growth targets. The speaker uses Cisco Systems as a cautionary tale of a company paid for the wrong things, contrasting it with high-quality businesses like Costco and Dollar General that possess durable competitive advantages and improving capital efficiency.

claims.claim: The speaker views Costco as a high-quality business with improving returns on capital and a long-term growth trajectory.
claims.quote: So fast forward to today, the business has grown the number of units to probably 800, just under 800. There are maybe 150 international stores in the mix. Returns on capital today are 21, 22%.

claims.claim: The speaker owns Dollar General because it is uniquely positioned against online commerce and has a strong management team.
claims.quote: And we think, for different reasons, Costco and Dollar General are two businesses that are uniquely positioned as impenetrable by online commerce. I mean, if Costco may do online commerce, Dollar General is running ads through their online model, but Dollar General is just a unique animal.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Dollar General will likely reach its target of 24 or 25,000 stores over the next 10 to 12 years.
claims.quote: And I think if they're running 15,000 stores today, at the time we did our original analysis, I think they talked about having 24 or 25,000 stores, I think they'll probably get there.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that 70% of Dollar General's business is in rural markets, which differentiates it from competitors and makes online shipping economics difficult.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Cisco Systems as an example of a company that has a hurdle for bonus comp related to organic sales growth.
claims.quote: Well, if you think about the nature of branding consumer goods businesses and the threats they have from private label, for example. If we go back 10 years ago, 12 years ago, these guys had in their proxy statement for bonus comp a hurdle of maybe 3% organic sales growth.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the hurdle for bonus comp at Cisco Systems declined from 3% to a negative 1.4% organic growth rate over time.
claims.quote: And in the successive period through this last year, that number had declined from 3 to 2, 2 to 1.5, 1 to 1.1.4. Well, the number today, the hurdle today is a negative 1.4% organic growth rate.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Cisco Systems pays performance comp based on free cash flow on a rolling three-year period.
claims.quote: The other overlay to the current comp, and this has evolved in the case of General Mills as well, is we're going to pay you on free cash on a rolling three-year period. They have an organic sales growth on a rolling rolling three. They have free cash on a rolling three.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems had a 50% mix between organic sales and free cash flow metrics for compensation.
claims.quote: So with one of their hurdles, there's a 50% mix between the organic sales, which they did not hit for a rolling three. So they got zero. But then they had 132% of the free cash metric. They paid that pro rata.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Cisco Systems paid 66% of the compensation due to the mix of metrics, even though they did not hit the organic sales target.
claims.quote: They split the 132%. So they paid 66%. They didn't get zero and 100 for 50. They actually got 66, which is crazy.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems does not have a return on capital metric in their proxy statement.
claims.quote: So the thing that goes missing from a proxy like that, which we see in too many places, Coca-Cola is another example of it. Too many businesses don't have a return on capital. They don't have an asset-based return metric.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Cisco Systems is paid for nonsensical things like top-line growth rather than capital-based returns.
claims.quote: They don't have an equity-based return metric. They don't have a capital-based return metric. They're paid for all kinds of nonsistical things like top-line growth. So what does the General Mills do in the wake of all that?

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems bought Blue Buffalo for $8 billion for $1.2 billion in revenues.
claims.quote: Well, they're not hitting the portion of comp that's tied to organic growth. So you buy Blue Buffalo. You pay something like $8 billion for $1.2 billion in revenues. It might be a good deal. It might not.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Cisco Systems does not get the calculation for comp in the first year they make an acquisition.
claims.quote: So you don't get the calculation for comp in the first year you make an acquisition, but you have a business that's clearly growing the top line and they're going to drive top-line growth.

claims.claim: The speaker questions whether the premium paid for Blue Buffalo is too big of a premium for that brand to be a creative on a return on capital basis.
claims.quote: Is it profitable? I don't know. Is that too big of a premium for that brand to be a creative on a return on capital basis? It doesn't matter because that's not part of the metric on how they pay themselves.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems has a notion of high incremental return on capital as a common attribute to look for in a business.
claims.quote: You've already kind of danced around one, which is this notion of high incremental return on capital. And you also alluded to this idea with some of the stores, raw stores as an example of sort of unit by unit expansion as being a really simple example of high returns on a new store, let's say.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems has a great example of incremental return on capital with Ross.
claims.quote: So I do have a great example of that. So we made the big mistake with Ross. We didn't know it was a mistake at the time, of course. But a couple of years after we sell Ross, I think maybe 2000 and four, we buy Costco for the first time.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems sold Ross at 20 times earnings.
claims.quote: We sold things at 20 times earnings. 20 times was nosebleed. I pay 20 times earnings for Costco. Because with it, we had a business that looked similar to a Ross.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems believed Costco had a very long ramp to open stores.
claims.quote: But we believed Costco had a very long ramp to open stores. They were just beginning to pay a small portion of their profit as dividends. So you wondered, well, is this thing getting closer to maturity or not.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems knew that a new Costco store would not earn 11 on capital right out of the gate.
claims.quote: In the case of a Costco, a store wouldn't earn 11 on capital right out of the gate. They're brand new stores were earning kind of mid to high single digit returns on capital, but the mature stores were earning kind of mid-teens returns.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems figured 11 was the wrong number for Costco's returns on capital.
claims.quote: And so we figured 11 was the wrong number and as the installed base of Costco, for lack of the number of stores they were opening, you would start to see the improvements and returns on capital.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Cisco Systems baked in a high teens return on capital business for Costco.
claims.quote: And I think two or three points of that is probably due to the tax code change. When I look at Costco today, we kind of bake in kind of a high teens, call it 18 or a 19 return on capital business.
